strengths: The paper addresses an important robotics bottleneck: reducing the manual effort required to construct symbolic planning domains and connect them to motion planners.

The combination of simulation-derived predicate constraints, LLM-based action induction, symbolic search, and the Logical Constraint Adapter is intuitive and potentially useful. The resulting domains are also more interpretable than purely language-based plans.

The simulation study is broad in surface coverage, reporting more than 1,200 tasks across nine environments, long planning horizons, multiple time limits, prompt variations, and several LLM-planning baselines.

The reported planning success is strong: PDDLLM substantially outperforms the tested LLM planners and approaches the reported expert-domain performance. Demonstrations on three physical robot platforms further support practical relevance.
weaknesses: The central claim that a reliable, complete planning domain can be derived “from scratch” from one demonstration is not technically justified. A single positive trajectory cannot identify necessary versus incidental preconditions, unobserved effects, or actions absent from that trajectory. The approach additionally assumes a predefined continuous feature representation, feature bounds and partitions, object identities and properties, a simulator, scene-description templates, and a motion-planning stack; the amount of task-specific engineering needed for these inputs is not quantified.

The “single demonstration” framing is inconsistent with the evaluation. Rearrangement combines stacking and unstacking demonstrations, bridge building combines stacking and alignment demonstrations, and the robustness experiment incrementally aggregates several action demonstrations. Consequently, the strongest compositional results do not establish the headline single-demonstration claim.

The domain-learning evaluation lacks the most relevant comparisons. The main baselines are direct LLM task planners rather than competing domain-inference or predicate/action-learning methods discussed in related work. They receive natural-language demonstrations and rely on predefined skills, whereas PDDLLM receives structured state trajectories, simulation access, generated domains, and a symbolic solver. This asymmetry makes the large performance gap insufficient evidence of superior domain induction.

The expert baseline is not independent: its domains are explicitly initialized from and refined from PDDLLM outputs. It therefore cannot serve convincingly as a ground-truth upper bound, and comparison with it may conceal errors shared with the generated domains.

Predicate imagination is underspecified and appears brittle. Grid partitioning scales exponentially with feature dimension; the proposed decomposition can discard cross-feature relations. LLM-assigned names do not establish semantic correctness, and examples include nonstandard or apparently invalid PDDL-like quantified expressions. The paper does not measure predicate precision/recall, classifier accuracy, action-schema correctness, or validity on held-out transitions.

LoCA's correctness claim is too strong. It retrieves constraints only from first-order predicates in an action's effect set, but the paper does not explain how it handles negative or quantified effects, delete effects, path-wide collision constraints, contact dynamics, or effects that are not geometric terminal-state constraints. Satisfying selected terminal inequalities does not by itself guarantee semantically correct action execution.

The ablations are insufficient to identify which components matter. There is no controlled removal of simulation verification, relevance filtering, higher-order predicate construction, parallel prompting, action refinement, or LoCA, nor a comparison against simpler trajectory-differencing and hand-specified discretization approaches.

Experimental reporting is not reproducible enough. The appendix mostly gives short task descriptions rather than exact instance generators, goals, demonstrations, success criteria, feature partitions, simulator parameters, prompts for complete domains, or generated PDDL files. Only three runs are used, and the origin of uncertainty estimates and per-task sample counts is unclear. No code or artifact release is stated.

The physical-robot evidence is qualitative image sequences without trial counts, success rates, failure analysis, or comparisons. The VLA policy is fine-tuned on 200 trajectories, further weakening any conclusion that the displayed behavior follows from one demonstration or from automatic domain derivation alone.

Efficiency comparisons omit or inadequately amortize the potentially substantial offline cost of thousands of simulation rollouts and many parallel LLM prompts. Token totals are difficult to interpret across one-time domain construction and per-instance planning, so the claimed deployment advantage is not established.

Several presentation and consistency issues reduce confidence, including contradictory or confusing labels in the missing-demonstration experiment, a duplicated baseline label in the timing table, sparse real-robot documentation, and overly broad claims of completeness, guarantees, and scalability that are not supported by the presented analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in task-and-motion planning: reducing the manual effort required to construct symbolic domains and connect them to continuous motion planning.
Combining simulated interaction, LLM-based predicate/action naming, symbolic planning, and the LoCA constraint interface is an intuitively appealing system contribution.
The simulated evaluation is broad in surface scope, covering nine environments, over 1,200 problem instances, varying object counts, long plans, prompt variations, and multiple planning-time limits.
PDDLLM reports strong simulated planning success, including difficult compositional settings, and the generated representations are human-interpretable.
Demonstrations on three physical robot platforms and compatibility with a learned VLA execution policy provide useful qualitative evidence of system flexibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of constructing domains "from scratch" without manual predesign is overstated. The method assumes a hand-specified feature space and bounds, discretization intervals, exact object states, a simulator, scene-description templates, task descriptions, and a compatible motion-planning representation. Much of the predicate grounding is obtained directly from manually chosen feature partitions; the LLM primarily assigns semantic names and relevance labels to these bins.

The "single demonstration" framing is misleading for compositional tasks. Rearrangement combines stacking and unstacking demonstrations, bridge building combines stacking and alignment, and the robustness experiment incrementally supplies pick, stack, and align trajectories. The paper does not clearly specify whether the claim means one demonstration per primitive, per environment, or per final domain.

The action-invention procedure is technically under-specified and not convincingly validated. Inferring general preconditions and effects from one observed transition is fundamentally ambiguous and can introduce accidental preconditions or omit necessary effects. There is no systematic test of learned transition-model accuracy on unseen transitions, nor comparison with ground-truth actions beyond coarse missing/redundant percentages.

Several formal details are questionable or incomplete. The examples mix nonstandard notation with PDDL, quantified expressions are apparently treated as ordinary predicates, and it is unclear how these constructs are compiled for the stated solver. Likewise, retrieving constraints only from positive first-order effects does not establish the claimed guarantee that an executed trajectory realizes the full symbolic action, especially for negative, quantified, contact, holding, and sequential effects.

The baseline set does not adequately support the main domain-induction claim. Most comparisons are against direct LLM task planners, which solve a different problem and predictably lack the advantage of symbolic search. Relevant predicate/action or planning-domain learning methods discussed in related work are not experimentally compared. The "Expert" domain is also created by refining PDDLLM's output rather than being an independent expert construction.

Cost and efficiency comparisons are not well controlled. The reported online planning time appears to exclude the substantial offline simulation and domain-generation process, while the token table does not clearly explain amortization over tasks. PDDLLM uses substantially more tokens than the standard GPT-4o baseline, so the broad claim of reduced token cost only holds against selected reasoning-model variants.

The 1,200-task evaluation lacks crucial experimental detail: exact instance counts and distributions per condition, train/development/test separation, whether refinement or candidate selection accesses evaluation problems, definitions of planning versus execution success, sources of randomness, and how the reported standard errors are calculated. These omissions make leakage, fairness, and statistical reliability difficult to assess.

The real-robot evidence is qualitative: no number of trials, success rates, baseline comparisons, failure analysis, or domain-generation measurements are reported. Images of successful executions are insufficient to substantiate robust cross-platform deployment.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript does not provide code or generated domains, exact LLM versions and decoding settings, complete task assets, feature partitions and hyperparameters, simulation-rollout counts, candidate-selection/refinement algorithms, or enough LoCA implementation detail to reproduce the principal results.

The scalability argument overlooks growth with object tuples, predicate arity, feature combinations, exhaustive higher-order predicate construction, and simulator rollouts. Demonstrating at most roughly 150 predicates and 20 objects does not justify the paper's broader scalability claims. Overall, the idea is promising, but the unsupported automation claims, mismatched comparisons, and insufficiently specified evaluation constitute substantial weaknesses for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: PDDLLM addresses an important bottleneck in task-and-motion planning: constructing interpretable symbolic domains and connecting them to continuous execution with less manual engineering.
The combination of simulation-grounded predicate generation, demonstration-based action induction, and the Logical Constraint Adapter is conceptually appealing and potentially useful.
The evaluation is broad in scale, covering over 1,200 problems across nine simulated environments, planning horizons reportedly reaching 510 actions, several time limits, and three robot platforms.
Reported planning performance is strong: PDDLLM substantially outperforms the direct LLM-planning baselines and approaches the expert-refined domains across most tasks.
The paper includes useful analyses of task complexity, incomplete or noisy demonstrations, prompt variations, token usage, and compositional reuse of actions across tasks.
weaknesses: The central claim of deriving domains “from scratch” with no manual initialization is overstated. The system assumes a predefined continuous feature space, feature types and ranges, discretization intervals, object models, a simulator, perception functions, task descriptions, and motion-planning infrastructure. The amount of engineering needed to provide these ingredients is not quantified.

The principal baselines are direct LLM planners rather than competitive domain-learning or predicate-invention methods discussed in the related-work section. Consequently, the large performance gap partly demonstrates the established advantage of symbolic search over direct sequence generation, rather than isolating the quality of the proposed domain-derivation method.

Important implementation details are missing, including feature-partition hyperparameters, numbers and costs of simulation rollouts, candidate-domain selection criteria, action segmentation, pruning rules, and complete executable generated domains. Some displayed quantified predicates and actions are not valid standard PDDL, making the actual compilation procedure unclear.

The cost comparison is difficult to interpret because PDDLLM performs substantial one-time offline simulation and LLM prompting while baselines reason online. The manuscript does not report total domain-construction time, simulator calls, monetary cost, or the number of downstream problems needed to amortize this expense.

Evaluation of generation reliability is incomplete. Results are averaged over three runs, but it is unclear whether domains are regenerated independently or only planning randomness is repeated. Candidate replacement based on whether domains produce feasible plans may also introduce evaluation leakage unless refinement and held-out task sets are clearly separated.

The expert reference is not independent: its domains are initialized from PDDLLM outputs and then refined. Likewise, the missing/redundant predicate metric depends on comparison with these refined domains and a vaguely defined “significant” performance change, weakening the domain-quality conclusions.

The real-robot section supplies photographs and successful examples but no trial counts, success rates, failure analysis, or comparison. The VLA experiment uses a policy fine-tuned on 200 trajectories, which also qualifies the impression that deployment follows from only one demonstration.

There are no targeted ablations for simulation verification, higher-order predicate construction, feature discretization, action invention, or LoCA. In particular, sensitivity to interval size and evidence that LoCA handles more than terminal effect constraints are needed to support the broad automation and scalability claims.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in task-and-motion planning: reducing the manual effort required to construct symbolic domains and connect them to continuous execution.

The proposed combination of simulation-grounded predicate generation, LLM-based action induction, symbolic search, and the Logical Constraint Adapter is intuitive and potentially useful. Producing reusable domains rather than repeatedly querying an LLM is a sensible design choice.

The empirical scope is broad, covering nine simulated task families, object-count and time-limit variations, several LLM backbones, prompt and discretization ablations, and deployments on three robot platforms.

Reported planning success is strong and approaches the expert-domain baseline on many tasks. The appendices provide useful prompt examples, task descriptions, robustness analyses, and real-robot trial counts.

The method yields interpretable predicates and actions, and the experiments illustrate potentially valuable compositional transfer from simpler demonstrations to rearrangement and bridge-building tasks.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly validate the central domain-induction contribution. Most baselines are online LLM task planners rather than competing domain-learning methods, so the large success-rate advantage primarily demonstrates the known benefit of symbolic search with a reusable domain. Relevant learned-domain, predicate-invention, and language-to-PDDL approaches are discussed but not compared empirically.

The comparison is computationally asymmetric: PDDLLM's expensive offline domain construction, including ten parallel prompts, hundreds of thousands of tokens, thousands of simulations, candidate rejection, and LLM voting, is excluded from the planning-time limit, whereas the baselines must perform LLM reasoning within that limit. Consequently, the planning-time and token-efficiency claims are not apples-to-apples. PDDLLM also uses more tokens than GPT-4o LLMTAMP in every reported task.

The claimed end-to-end success rates appear not to account clearly for domain-generation failure. The appendix reports an 8.3% failure rate at the chosen ten-prompt setting, but it is unclear whether Table 1 conditions on an executable domain. Candidate domains are explicitly discarded using execution feedback, which may introduce substantial selection and test-environment leakage.

The claim of deriving a complete domain 'from scratch' from one demonstration is overstated. The system assumes a manually specified feature space and bounds, discretization scheme, object identities and CAD/URDF models, a reliable simulator and perception interface, task descriptions, prompt templates, a symbolic solver, and continuous constraints associated with sampled bins. In effect, much of the grounding structure is supplied in advance, while the LLM often assigns semantic names and relevance labels to predefined regions.

A single trajectory cannot in general identify action preconditions or distinguish causal conditions from coincidental state facts. The paper provides no identifiability assumptions or systematic intervention-based procedure to address this ambiguity, and action schemas are inferred directly from observed before/after states. The very high results therefore require stronger evidence against memorization, LLM prior knowledge, or environment-specific engineering.

The technical specification is incomplete and sometimes inconsistent. Several displayed 'PDDL' expressions are malformed or nonstandard; the construction and compilation of quantified predicates are not defined precisely; and generating all valid higher-order combinations is combinatorial. LoCA is described largely as retrieving constraints from action effects, without enough detail to establish how grasping, collision avoidance, path-wide constraints, preconditions, controller selection, or effects without direct geometric inequalities are handled. Thus the assertion that no predefined motion skills or engineered interface is needed is not adequately supported.

Generalization is evaluated mostly within the same nine designed domains using more objects. There is no clean held-out-domain evaluation with independently selected features, dynamics, or vocabulary. Rearrangement and bridge building also use multiple demonstrations of constituent skills, weakening the headline 'one demo is all it takes' characterization.

The expert baseline is not an independently authored ground-truth domain: it is obtained by refining PDDLLM outputs. Missing and redundant predicate percentages are therefore circular and are also defined operationally through performance rather than semantic correctness. Only four domains receive this analysis, despite claims about complete, high-quality domain induction.

Experimental reporting is insufficiently precise for reproducibility and statistical interpretation. The paper does not provide code, generated domains, problem instances, API/model snapshots, seeds, complete simulator settings, or a detailed accounting of the 1,200 tasks. It is unclear what the three runs vary, what sample sizes underlie each table entry, and whether uncertainty includes variation in domain generation. Some tables also contain labeling and numerical inconsistencies.

The real-robot evidence is encouraging but limited to ten trials per task with marker-based perception and only success counts. It does not isolate failures due to induced domains versus perception, motion planning, or execution, and the VLA experiment relies on a policy fine-tuned with 200 trajectories, complicating claims of minimal supervision and automatic low-level integration.

Overall, the idea is promising and the reported results are extensive, but the absence of appropriate domain-learning baselines, asymmetric accounting, unclear conditioning on successful domain generation, and under-specified technical pipeline prevent the evidence from supporting the paper's strongest claims at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The problem is important: reducing manual construction of symbolic task-and-motion-planning domains could materially improve robot-planning scalability.
The proposed combination of simulation-grounded predicate induction, LLM-based action abstraction, and the LoCA interface is conceptually interesting and produces human-readable representations.
The empirical scope is broad on paper, covering nine simulated task families, several planning horizons, prompt and hyperparameter ablations, three robot platforms, and multiple LLM backbones.
The paper discusses relevant limitations, including missing complex predicates, perception noise, and difficult-to-simulate dynamics.
weaknesses: The central claim of deriving a complete domain "from a single demonstration" is misleading. The system additionally assumes structured continuous states, manually specified feature types and ranges, CAD/URDF models, a physics simulator, task descriptions, scene templates, perception infrastructure, and thousands of simulated samples. Some complex tasks also use multiple demonstrations from different subtasks.

The symbolic formulation is technically unclear and sometimes invalid. Examples mix named negative predicates with PDDL negation, use expressions such as "forall ... is false" that are not valid PDDL, contain malformed parentheses and commas, and appear inconsistent with the declared STRIPS requirements. It is not explained how quantified summary predicates are correctly maintained after actions.

A single observed transition is generally insufficient to identify an action's necessary preconditions, effects, or causal structure. The paper provides no rigorous treatment of ambiguity, negative evidence, confounders, or how trajectory segmentation distinguishes intended action effects from incidental predicate changes.

LoCA is substantially underspecified. Retrieving inequalities associated with effect predicates does not by itself define grasps, collision-free transit and transfer motions, kinematics, contact modes, or controllers. Consequently, the claim that it removes predefined motion skills and guarantees semantically aligned executable trajectories is unsupported.

The evaluation lacks strong, faithful comparisons to existing domain-learning methods. Most baselines are locally constructed LLM planners "inspired by" prior work rather than implementations of competitive domain-induction systems, while the expert baseline is created by refining PDDLLM outputs and is therefore not an independent reference.

Critical experimental details are missing: exact task distributions, generated domains, simulator configurations, success-checking procedures, model snapshots and decoding settings, seeds, and sufficient per-condition sample counts. No code or data release is identified, making the unusually high success rates difficult to verify.

The domain-quality analysis is partly circular: the expert domains are initialized from PDDLLM outputs and then used to label PDDLLM predicates as missing or redundant. The operational thresholds for whether removal "significantly" changes performance are not specified, and this analysis covers only four tasks.

The headline token-efficiency comparison is not consistently favorable: GPT-4o LLMTAMP uses fewer tokens in every reported task. PDDLLM's offline domain-construction cost is compared with per-instance planning without a clear amortization analysis, despite requiring roughly 334k–535k tokens per domain.

The real-robot evidence is limited to ten trials for each of four settings, with no baseline, uncertainty analysis, task-distribution description, or evaluation of domain derivation itself. These demonstrations support feasibility but not the claimed cross-platform robustness or automation.

Several quantitative and conceptual inconsistencies reduce confidence. For example, reported results vary across tables without fully clear conditions, the search-complexity calculation treats the branching factor as m×n despite parameterized actions, and nearly identical results across GPT-4o and small Qwen models are not accompanied by domain-level analysis.

The ethics discussion states that no misuse is foreseeable, but autonomous robot planning can introduce physical safety risks. The paper does not discuss safeguards, failure containment, or risks from incorrectly inferred predicates and action models.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in task-and-motion planning: reducing the manual effort needed to construct symbolic domains and connect them to continuous execution.

PDDLLM is an appealing combination of LLM-based abstraction, physics-simulation feedback, symbolic planning, and constrained motion planning. The induced predicates and actions are interpretable, and the reuse of a derived domain can improve long-horizon planning efficiency.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: more than 1,200 problems across nine task families, complexity and time-limit analyses, prompt and hyperparameter ablations, multiple LLM backbones, perception-noise tests, and deployments on three physical robot platforms.

The reported planning results are strong. PDDLLM substantially outperforms the evaluated LLM planners and approaches the expert-domain baseline, including on challenging compositional tasks such as rearrangement, bridge building, and Tower of Hanoi.
The appendix provides prompts, task descriptions, real-robot success counts, token measurements, and several useful diagnostic experiments.
weaknesses: The headline claim of deriving a complete domain “from scratch” from one demonstration is overstated. The system assumes predefined continuous features, object identities and CAD/URDF information, scene-description templates, discretization machinery, a simulator, predicate evaluators, and a compatible constrained motion-planning stack. The true amount of task-specific engineering is not quantified.

LoCA is insufficiently specified to support the claim of fully automatic action-to-motion grounding. Retrieving constraints from action effects does not by itself explain grasp/release control, collision-free approach and retreat motions, action parameter binding, or predicates such as holding. Algorithmic details and a LoCA-specific ablation are needed for reproducibility and soundness.

The comparison set emphasizes direct LLM planners rather than the closest planning-domain or predicate-learning approaches cited by the paper. Those baselines also receive predefined execution skills, while PDDLLM's offline simulation and domain-construction costs are excluded from the 50-second planning comparison. Consequently, the results establish advantages for repeated planning with an induced domain, but not conclusively superior domain induction.

The token-efficiency claim needs qualification: PDDLLM uses roughly 415k tokens on average for the three complex tasks, versus about 10k for GPT-4o LLMTAMP, and is cheaper only than the reasoning-model variants. Domain-generation wall-clock time, simulator rollouts, API cost, and the number of test problems required to amortize this expense are not reported.

At the default ten parallel prompts, executable-domain generation still has an 8.3% failure rate. It is unclear whether such failures are included in the main success rates or whether those results condition on a successfully generated domain. Domain-generation trials, planning trials, and uncertainty estimates should be separated clearly.

The evaluation of domain quality uses an expert domain obtained by refining PDDLLM's output rather than an independently authored reference, which can bias missing/redundant-element comparisons. Moreover, those metrics are based on only four domains and their operational definitions depend on observed planning performance.

Important reproducibility details remain absent, including generated domain files and code, exact simulator-rollout counts and sampling procedures, domain-generation wall-clock costs, API/model versions and decoding settings, and sufficiently precise statistical accounting. Some presented PDDL examples also appear syntactically informal or invalid.

The real-robot evidence is encouraging but limited to ten trials per task with marker-based perception, and the VLA component is fine-tuned on 200 task-specific trajectories. This supports feasibility more than broad real-world autonomy.
